en: The *Upadeśa* on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Volume One.
Explained by the Mahāyāna Master Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of Northern India during the Later Wei dynasty.
I prostrate to the Ocean of Perfect Enlightenment, To the pure Dharma and the unconditioned Saṅgha;
For the sake of those with profound wisdom, I shall expound this treatise on grammar (Vyākaraṇa).
With utmost reverence, I pay homage to the Honored Muni, As well as to the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
To cause the Dharma to benefit both self and others, I briefly set forth this *Lakṣa-vibhaṅga*.
I take refuge in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present worlds;
may your great compassion descend with supernatural power, and grant me fearlessness.

Great Compassion halts the four Māras, Protecting and increasing Bodhi. Chapter One: Introduction Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.

All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, free from further afflictions, having attained mastery over their minds; they were well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom. Their minds were thoroughly tamed; they were great dragons among men. They had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished. They had laid down all heavy burdens and attained their own benefit. Having exhausted all fetters of existence, they were well-liberated through right knowledge and mental liberation; they had attained mastery over all their minds and reached the supreme further shore.

There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; all had attained dhāraṇīs and great eloquence in joyful exposition, and turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma. They had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas and planted various roots of goodness in the presence of those buddhas. They were constantly praised by all the buddhas, and they cultivated their bodies and minds through great compassion. They skillfully entered the wisdom of the buddhas, attained mastery of great knowledge, and reached the other shore. Their fame was heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and they were able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
The commentary states:
In the first chapter of this dharma-gate of the sutra, seven kinds of accomplishments of merit are manifested; this meaning should be understood.
What are these seven?
First, the accomplishment of the introductory section;
second, the accomplishment of the assembly;
third, the accomplishment of the arrival of the time when the Tathāgata intends to preach the Dharma.
Fourth, the accomplishment of abiding in accordance with the majestic deportment of the Dharma taught;
fifth, the accomplishment of relying on the causes for teaching;
sixth, the accomplishment of the great assembly being present and desiring to hear the Dharma.
Seventh is the accomplishment of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s response.

Regarding the accomplishment of the introductory section, one should understand that within this dharma-gate, two kinds of supreme accomplishment of ultimate meaning are revealed. This is the sense in which it should be known.
What are these two?
First, the accomplishment of the meaning of the most supreme among all dharma-gates;
second, the accomplishment of the meaning of the qualities of mastery.
Just as Rājagṛha excels all other cities and Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain excels all other mountains, this Dharma-gate is manifested as being of the most supreme significance.
As it says in the Sūtra: "The Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Regarding the accomplishment of the assembly, it should be understood that this manifestation of accomplishment possesses four kinds of meanings.
What are the four? First, accomplishment in number;
second, accomplishment in practice.
Third is the accomplishment of gathering merit;
fourth is the accomplishment of abiding in majestic deportment according to the Dharma.
As for the accomplishment of number, it is because the great assembly is incalculable.
There are four types of those who accomplish practice:
first, those śrāvakas who cultivate the practices of the Hīnayāna;
second, those bodhisattvas who cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna.

Third, it refers to those bodhisattvas who, possessing mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifest at will and are able to practice the Mahāyāna, such as the sixteen great virtuous men beginning with Śrīghoṣa Bodhisattva; they are fully endowed with the inconceivable deeds of a bodhisattva and constantly manifest various forms, such as upāsakas, upāsikās, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs.
Fourth, it refers to the fact that the deportment (*īryāpatha*) of ordained śrāvakas is fixed and uniform, which differs from that of bodhisattvas.
The sixteen phrases beginning with "All are arhats" demonstrate the accomplishment of the merits of the śrāvakas.
The thirteen phrases beginning with "All are non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" demonstrate the accomplishment of the merits of the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the accomplishment of the qualities of the śrāvakas, it should be understood that the meaning is demonstrated through sixteen phrases subsumed under three categories.
What are these three categories?
First, the category of progressive arising (uttarottara-utpatti-mukha).
Second is the gate of general and specific characteristics;
third is the gate of encompassing phenomena.
Regarding the gate of progressive arising: because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, one is called an Arhat.
Because the mind has attained mastery, it is said that "all outflows are exhausted.
Because there are no further afflictions, it is said that "the mind has attained mastery.
Because one has well attained liberation of mind and well attained liberation through wisdom, it is said that "the mind has attained mastery."
Because one is far removed from both the seer and the seen, it is called "no further afflictions.
Because one has well attained liberation of mind and well attained liberation through wisdom, it is called "the mind being well-tamed."
The great dragon among men travels through all evil paths as if on a level road, without any obstruction,
because he has already traversed what was to be traversed and has already reached what was to be reached.
He has performed what was to be done, for he is a great dragon among men who has attained the remedies to subdue the enemy that is affliction.
He has accomplished his task, for he will not be born again, as the matters corresponding to his purpose have already been perfected.
"Having laid down all heavy burdens" means that one has performed what was to be done and accomplished what was to be achieved, thereby having already cast off the heavy burden of future rebirth.
"Attaining one's own benefit" means that, having already laid down the burden, one has realized nirvana.
"One who has exhausted all fetters of existence" is so called because they have attained their own benefit by severing the causes of all afflictions.
"One who has well-attained right knowledge and liberation of mind" is so called because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted.
Those who have attained mastery over all minds do so because they skillfully know and see the wisdom of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

Those who have reached the supreme further shore do so because they have skillfully attained the liberation of mind through right knowledge, as well as various meritorious qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
Regarding "the great arhats and so forth," it is because they have attained mastery over the mind and reached the further shore.
Regarding "those known by all," it is because kings, princes, ministers, commoners, Śakra, the king of gods, Brahmā, the king of gods, and others all recognize them.
Furthermore, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, buddhas, and others are superior wise ones; since those superior wise ones all thoroughly know him, he is therefore called "one known by the multitude."
Regarding the section on the general and specific characteristics, there are sixteen phrases beginning with "All are arhats.
The first phrase is the general [characteristic], while the remaining phrases are the specific ones.
That which is called an "arhat" (worthy one) should be understood as having fifteen kinds of meanings of "worthiness."
What are these fifteen?
First, because he is worthy of receiving offerings of food, drink, bedding, and seats, as well as honor and respect;
second, because he should lead the great assembly to teach and transform all beings.
Third, because one should enter villages, cities, and so forth;
fourth, because one should subdue various non-Buddhists and others;
fifth, because one should swiftly observe phenomena with wisdom.
Sixth, one should preach the Dharma neither too hastily nor too slowly, in accordance with the Dharma, without becoming weary;
seventh, one should sit in quiet seclusion, not accumulating or hoarding food, clothing, or any necessities of life, because of having few desires and being content;
eighth, one should practice exclusively wholesome conduct, without becoming attached to the various dhyānas.
Ninth, because one should practice the noble conduct of emptiness;
tenth, because one should practice the noble conduct of signlessness;
eleventh, because one should practice the noble conduct of wishlessness.
Twelfth, because one should subdue the mundane mind through pure dhyāna;
thirteenth, because one should give rise to the supreme merit of the various supernormal powers (abhijñā);
fourteenth, because one should realize the supreme merit of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Fifteenth, one should know things as they truly are: that all beings born together attain various merits for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Regarding the "gate of gathering matters," it should be understood that these fifteen phrases encompass ten kinds of merit, demonstrating both expressible and inexpressible fruits.
What are the ten?
First is the manifestation of the two phrases concerning the merit of gathering virtues, as stated in the Sūtra: "All outflows are exhausted, and there are no further afflictions."
Second, the three phrases encompass all merits:
one phrase concerns the merit of subduing the world, as in the sutra’s statement, “the mind attains mastery”;
two phrases concern the merit of subduing those in training who transcend the world, as in the sutra’s statement, “well-attained liberation of mind and well-attained liberation through wisdom.”
Third is the inclusion of the merit of non-contradiction, because one acts in accordance with the Tathāgata’s teachings, as the sūtra says, "the mind is well-tamed.
Fourth is the inclusion of superior merit, as the sūtra says, "a great dragon among men."

Fifth is the grasping of the supreme merit that ought to be performed; "that which ought to be performed" refers to being able to make offerings to, revere, and honor the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dharma, as the sūtra states: "one performs what ought to be performed."
Sixth is the inclusion of the perfection of merit, because the stage of training is fulfilled, as the sūtra says, "What was to be done has been accomplished.
Seventh is the inclusion of the merit of transcendence through three phrases:
first, the transcendence of craving; [the others follow].
Second, the transcendence of seeking offerings, livelihood, and honor;
third, the transcendence of the lower and upper realms, because one has already transcended the stages of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says: "Because they have abandoned all heavy burdens," "because they have attained their own benefit," and "because they have exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*)."
Eighth is the inclusion of the supreme and unsurpassed merit, as the sūtra says: "Having well attained right knowledge and liberation of mind.
Ninth is the inclusion of the merit of performing beneficial deeds for sentient beings, as the sūtra says: "Attaining mastery over all minds."
Tenth is the merit of grasping the foremost [qualities], as the sūtra says, "reaching the first shore.
It should be understood that the accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s merits is demonstrated through thirteen phrases, which are shown to be subsumed under two categories.
What are these two gates?
First, the gate of the upper and lower branches;
second, the gate of the inclusion of matters.

Regarding the section on the upper and lower branches: this refers to the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), which should be understood as follows.
"All [of them] do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" is the general characteristic; the remainder are the specific characteristics.
One should understand that there are ten manifestations of non-retrogression; what are these ten?
First is abiding in the non-retrogression of hearing the Dharma, as the sutra states: "They all attain dhāraṇīs."
Second is the non-retrogression of eloquence, as the sutra says, "great eloquence and joyful speech.
Third is the non-retrogression of teaching, as the sutra says, "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma."

Fourth is non-retrogression by relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), because one relies on the physical body (*rūpakāya*) through the activities of body and mind; as the sūtra says, "making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" and "planting various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the presence of those Buddhas."
Fifth is the non-retrogression of severing all doubts, as the sutra says: "They are constantly praised by all Buddhas.

Sixth is the non-retrogression of entering into each respective teaching according to whatever matters one expounds for them, as the sutra says: "They cultivate their body and mind through great compassion."
Seventh is the non-retrogression in entering the reality-boundary of omniscience, as the sūtra says, "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom.
Eighth is the non-retrogression based on the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena, as the sūtra says, "penetrating great wisdom."
Ninth is non-retrogression in entering the realm of reality as it truly is, as the sutra says, "reaching the other shore.
Tenth is non-retrogression in performing what ought to be done, as the sutra says, "being able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."
Regarding the gate of grasping the subject matter: it demonstrates in which pure stages the bodhisattvas abide, by what means they act, and within what spheres of activity they perform their duties.
Regarding the purity of the stages (*bhūmi-pariśuddhi*): it refers to the tranquility and purity of signless practice (*animitta-caryā*) in the three stages from the eighth stage upward.
There are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*):
first, the skillful means of grasping the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*), which consists of upholding the sublime Dharma and expounding it for others through the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Second is the skillful means of embracing spiritual friends, because one performs what ought to be done by relying upon spiritual friends.
Third is the skillful means of embracing sentient beings, because one does not abandon sentient beings.
Fourth is the skillful means of encompassing wisdom (*jñāna-upāya*), because it teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may enter into that wisdom.

Furthermore, there is yet another door of encompassing activities, which manifests the distinct excellence of the merits encompassed by the various stages (*bhūmi*), as these differ from the merits of the two vehicles (*yāna*).
This refers to the non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) within the eighth stage, which is distinct from both the lower and the upper stages.
It is not like the lower because it cannot be moved by the practices involving effort;
it is not like the upper because it cannot be moved by signless practices, as it proceeds spontaneously.
In the ninth stage, one attains the *dhāraṇī* gate of supreme progress, because of being fully endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded sovereign wisdom.

In the tenth stage, one receives the rank of Buddha through the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma, just like the crown prince of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), because of attaining the same meaning of encompassing merit.
Regarding the accomplishment of the gathering of merits, it is shown by way of what basis, what mind, what wisdom, what sphere of activity, and what capacity for accomplishment.
As for what they rely upon, it is by relying on virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As for what their mind relies upon, it is by relying on the mind that transforms sentient beings, ultimately benefiting all sentient beings.
Regarding "by what wisdom": it is by means of three kinds of wisdom:
first, the secret wisdom of bestowing predictions; second, the wisdom of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); [and third, the wisdom of the knowledge of others' minds].
Third is true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
One should understand that it is comprised of three types of wisdom according to the objects upon which it acts and the means by which it accomplishes its purpose.
The accomplishment of abiding in conduct according to the Dharma consists of four kinds of manifestations.
What are the four? First, being surrounded by a multitude;
second, [being followed] before and behind.
Third is making offerings and showing respect;
fourth is honoring and praising.
As the sutra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, respected him, honored him, and praised him."
Regarding the phrase "when the Tathāgata wishes to preach the Dharma, it reaches fulfillment": this is for the purpose of preaching Mahāyāna sūtras to the bodhisattvas.
It should be understood that this Mahāyāna sūtra has seventeen names which manifest its profound merits.
What are these seventeen?
How are they manifested?
First, as for the name *Ananta-artha-sūtra*, it is because it accomplishes the meaning of the words; that is, by means of this Dharma-door, it expounds that profound and wondrous realm of phenomena.
That which is the profound Dharma and sublime realm is the most supreme realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Second, it is called the "Most Supreme Sūtra" because this Dharma-gate is perfectly accomplished within the most supreme and wondrous treasury among the Three Piṭakas.

The three are called "Vaipulya Sūtras" because they are well-accomplished within the gates of the immeasurable Mahāyāna, and because they are accomplished through abiding in accordance with the faculties of sentient beings.

The fourth is called "the teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma," because it serves to skillfully bring to maturity those bodhisattvas whose faculties have ripened, in accordance with their capacity as vessels for the Dharma.
The fifth is called "those protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha," because this Dharma exists by virtue of relying upon the Tathāgata.
Sixth, it is called "The Secret Dharma of All Buddhas," because this dharma is extremely profound and is known only by the Buddhas.
Seventh, it is called "The Treasury of All Buddhas," because the treasury of the Tathāgatas' merits and samādhis is contained within this sutra.
The eighth is called "the secret locus of all Buddhas," because it is not bestowed upon those whose faculties are immature or who are not vessels for receiving the Dharma.
The ninth is called "that which can give birth to the sūtras of all Buddhas," because by hearing this Dharma-gate, one can achieve the great Bodhi of all Buddhas.
The tenth is called "the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas," because this dharma-gate can bring about the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas, whereas other sūtras cannot.
Eleventh, it is named "The Wheel of Dharma Turned by All Buddhas," because this dharma-gate can destroy all obstacles.
Twelfth, it is named "The Solid Relics of All Buddhas," meaning that the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya* is not destroyed within this *sūtra*.

The thirteenth is titled *The Sūtra of the Great Skillful Means of All Buddhas*, so called because, having realized great bodhi by relying on this dharma-gate, one preaches all wholesome dharmas—such as those for devas, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—for the sake of sentient beings.

The fourteenth is named "Expounding the Sūtra of the One Vehicle," because this dharma-gate reveals the ultimate essence of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas the paths of the two vehicles are not ultimate.
The fifteenth is named "Abiding in the Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha-vihāra), because this Dharma-gate is the ultimate dwelling place of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The sixteenth is named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma); it has two meanings.
What are these two meanings?
First is the meaning of "emerging from water," because they have irreversibly emerged from the turbid waters of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Furthermore, there is another meaning: like the metaphor of a lotus emerging from mud and water, the śrāvakas enter and sit within the great assembly of the Tathāgata; just as bodhisattvas sit upon lotuses, they hear the exposition of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom and pure realm, thereby attaining realization of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury.

Second is the meaning of the blossoming of the flower: because sentient beings are timid and weak-minded regarding the Mahāyāna and are unable to give rise to faith, the pure and wondrous *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is revealed so that they may develop faith.
The seventeenth is called the "Supreme Dharma Gate" because it encompasses accomplishment.
To encompass accomplishment means to include immeasurable bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, such as the *vibhāṣā*, *akṣobhya*, and other *śloka* verses.
These seventeen phrases constitute the general [teaching], while the remaining phrases are the specific [teachings].
This is as stated in the sutra: "For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled 'The Immeasurable Meanings,'" and so forth.
Regarding the accomplishment of dwelling in accordance with the majestic deportment of the taught Dharma, it demonstrates by means of which specific dharmas one teaches the Dharma;
it is by means of three kinds of dharmas:
first, accomplishment based on samādhi.
The accomplishment of samādhi is manifested in two ways:
first, the accomplishment of sovereign power, because body and mind are immovable;
second, the departure from all obstacles, by virtue of following that sovereign power.
This power of mastery is further of two kinds:
first, to accord with sentient beings by not perceiving [the need for] antidotes while gathering the factors of enlightenment;
second, to serve as an antidote to the afflictions that have been firmly grasped throughout immeasurable lifetimes.

As it is said in the sutra: "After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, remaining unmoving in body and mind," and so forth.

The second is based on the receptacle world (bhājanaloka), and the third is based on the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka); this is because [the Buddha] causes the world to tremble and knows the events of immeasurable kalpas in the past, and so forth.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, continuing in succession until [the assembly] rejoiced, joined their palms, and with a single mind gazed upon the Buddha.

Regarding the accomplishment of the causes for this teaching, the Tathāgata manifested extraordinary and inconceivable phenomena for the great assembly. Having seen these, the assembly conceived a sense of wonder and, out of longing to hear [the Dharma], gave rise to this thought:
"The Tathāgata should now speak for my sake."
Therefore, this is called the accomplishment of the causal basis for the teaching.

For this reason, the Tathāgata emits great radiance to manifest various matters within the worlds of other directions; first, he manifests external phenomena for the great assembly, such as the sixfold earthquake, and subsequently, he manifests the profoundly deep and subtle, secret Dharma realized internally within this Dharma-gate. Furthermore, based upon the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) and the sentient-being world (*sattva-loka*), he manifests the Three Jewels through their various numbers and various magnitudes, including the distinctions of those possessed of afflictions, the distinctions of those possessed of purity, and the distinctions between the Buddhas and their disciples.

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions of vehicles, there are worlds where a Buddha exists and worlds where no Buddha exists; this causes sentient beings to see those who practice but have not yet attained the fruit, and those who have realized the Way and have already attained the fruit.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Those who practice and attain the Way.
Regarding the various enumerations, this demonstrates the various contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of contemplation:
First, eating;
second, hearing the Dharma;
third, practicing.
The fourth is joy (*sukha*).

As the sūtra states: "At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which proceeded in succession until stūpas made of the seven precious substances were erected for the Buddha’s relics."

One who practices the bodhisattva path should understand this principle: that they teach and transform sentient beings by skillfully gathering them through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
As it is taught in the sūtras, one should infer and apply this for oneself.
From this point onward, it is shown that the great assembly desires to hear the realization manifested before them.

As for questioning a single person, it causes many people to give rise to a sense of wonder at what they wish to hear; therefore, he questions Mañjuśrī alone, thus demonstrating that the World-Honored One’s disciples accord with the Dharma and do not contradict it.
What is the meaning of the present manifestation of supernatural transformations by the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
It is for the purpose of proclaiming the Great Dharma; he manifests these great signs as the causal basis for that proclamation.

He manifests these great signs because he is about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and he manifests these great auspicious omens because he is about to proclaim the inconceivable and other such words and phrases regarding the wondrous Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
There are two reasons for thus extolling Mañjuśrī. What are these two?
First, because he has directly perceived all dharmas.
Second, because those dharmas are accomplished solely within one's own internal mind, independent of all external causes and conditions.
As for the manifestation of various auspicious signs, it is for the purpose of manifesting various specific matters.
One should thoroughly understand how those phenomena appear, disappear, abide, and cease;
for Mañjuśrī is able to record those phenomena, and because he directly perceives those dharmas through the accomplishment of his deeds and the accomplishment of cause and effect.
Regarding the accomplishment of what is to be done, there are two kinds:
first, the accomplishment of merit;
second, the accomplishment of wisdom.
As for the accomplishment through causes, it is because of the accomplishment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Furthermore, there is another cause, namely the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*).
As for the accomplishment through causal conditions, it is because of the perfection of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for the accomplishment of the fruit, it is because he teaches the Great Dharma.
Regarding the various and diverse Buddha-lands, it should be understood that these are manifested for this purpose, showing the various and diverse distinctions within those lands.
A "pure and wondrous land" refers to the dwelling place of sentient beings who are free from afflictions.
This is as stated in the sutra: "It illuminates eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, proceeding in succession until all the adornments of those Buddha-lands are seen."
The Tathāgata is the foremost because all the bodhisattvas and others dwell in reliance upon the Tathāgata, as that Tathāgata has attained mastery among the great assemblies in that land.
As it is said in the sutra, "Furthermore, he sees the Buddhas currently residing in those lands," and so forth.
From this point onward, the text next clarifies the noble one.

Mañjuśrī, through his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), directly perceives the causal signs and resultant signs of the past as being fully accomplished, as if they were present before him; for this reason, he is able to answer Maitreya Bodhisattva.
What is the direct perception of the characteristics of past causes?
It refers to Mañjuśrī’s own perception of his own body, having practiced in various places throughout those respective lands by means of diverse deeds.
How is it that one directly perceives the signs of past fruits?

It is because Mañjuśrī himself saw his own body as the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Sudarśana) in a past life, who heard this Dharma-gate from that Buddha and preached it for the sake of sentient beings.
What are the ten matters that are accomplished?
First, the accomplishment of the cause for directly perceiving the great purpose;
second, the accomplishment of the cause for directly perceiving that the meaning of the world’s words, letters, and phrases is profoundly deep.
Third, the accomplishment of the cause of manifesting rare wonders;
fourth, the accomplishment of the cause of manifesting supreme excellence;
fifth, the accomplishment of the cause of manifesting great enjoyment.
Sixth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly seeing the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas;
seventh, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly seeing the well-established and solid wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata;
eighth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly seeing the ability to enter [the path].
Ninth is the accomplishment of the cause through present observation and recollection;
tenth is the accomplishment of the cause through present observation of the events experienced by oneself.
It should be understood that these eight phrases manifest the accomplishment of the cause of great purpose.
What are the eight? First, the desire to discourse upon the Great Dharma;
second, the desire to rain down the great rain of the Dharma;
Third, they desire to beat the great Dharma drum;
fourth, they desire to erect the great Dharma banner;
fifth, they desire to light the great Dharma lamp.
Sixth, he wishes to blow the great Dharma conch;
seventh, he wishes to beat the great Dharma drum without interruption;
eighth, he wishes to preach the Great Dharma.
These eight phrases are intended to demonstrate that the Tathāgata desires to discourse upon the Great Dharma and so forth.
What are the eight kinds of great meanings?
They are for the purpose of severing the doubts of those who have them.

Because those who have already severed doubt increase and bring to maturity that body of wisdom, for those whose faculties are matured, he explains two kinds of subtle and secret realms: first, the subtle and secret realm of the śrāvakas;
[second, the subtle and secret realm of the bodhisattvas].
Second is the subtle and secret realm of the Bodhisattva.
The two phrases concerning the "Great Dharma Drum" demonstrate that it is heard from afar.
As for "entering the secret realm," it causes them to advance toward the increasingly superior meaning of purity.
Regarding the supreme and most excellent meaning of pure progress: it is so that they may progress toward the realization of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) through direct perception.
That they may progress toward the realization of all-aspect omniscience through direct perception is for the purpose of establishing names, phrases, and meanings for all phenomena.
The purpose of establishing names, phrases, and meanings is to cause others to enter the turning of the wheel of Dharma through the realization-wisdom that is ineffable.

That the meaning of names, phrases, and sentences in the world is seen to be achieved through profound causes is as stated in the Sūtra: "I have previously witnessed this omen among the Buddhas of the past," continuing in sequence until, "therefore, I now manifest this omen."
The manifestation of the accomplishment of rare causes is such that they cannot be obtained even in immeasurable time.
That which is inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable is shown to transcend those incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and thus cannot be obtained.
Furthermore, he manifests five kinds of kalpas—namely, first, a night; second, a day; third, a month; fourth, a season; and fifth, a year—in order to manifest the immeasurable and boundless dharmas.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa; [the text continues] in succession until he caused [beings] to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus it is said.
Regarding the manifestation of the accomplishment of the supreme and wondrous causes, this is shown by the self-enjoyment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As the sutra states: "Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa, and so on in succession until: 'the Dharma he taught was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.'"

As for the accomplishment of the great cause of manifest enjoyment: at that time, the princes, having experienced supreme and wondrous bliss, each renounced their homes to leave the household life; furthermore, because the great assembly’s minds did not grow weary throughout that duration.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "When that final Buddha had not yet left the household life, and after proceeding in sequence until he had bestowed the prophecy of Buddhahood, he entered parinirvāṇa without remainder in the middle of the night."
The manifestation and perception of the accomplishment of the causes for all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma occurs because the wheel of Dharma is never interrupted.
As the sutra states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas."

The manifestation of the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma as being well-established and substantial through the accomplishment of its causes is because it is taught for immeasurable periods after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

As the sutra states: “The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Subhāṣitaratnagarbha as their teacher, and in succession, he caused them all to become firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
The manifestation of the accomplishment of the causes for entry is because those princes attain great bodhi;
as the sūtra says: "These princes, in succession, even until all have attained the path of buddhahood."
The accomplishment of the causes for present recollection is for the purpose of teaching the Dharma to others and benefiting them.
As the Sūtra says: "The last one to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara; [the others followed] in succession up to those who were honored and praised."
The accomplishment of the causes for what one personally experiences is due to one’s own reception of supreme and wondrous bliss.
This is as stated in the Sūtra: "Maitreya, you should know that this proceeds in succession until one is protected by the Buddhas."
You, who are named "Seeker of Fame," manifest the knowledge of those past events; furthermore, you manifest that the Dharma has now been attained in its entirety.
Moreover, it is based on the inclusion of the three meanings:
first, the act of bestowing the teaching, as in the sūtra: "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wishes to preach the Great Dharma," and so forth.
2. Because it establishes the teaching as it truly is, as the sūtra says: "In the past, I have seen... and so forth. 3.
Because it causes one to wait for the teaching, as the sūtra says: "All you people, you should now know... and so forth.
From this point onward, it is shown that the Dharma taught corresponds to its causes and effects;
this should be understood. Chapter Two: The Chapter on Expedient Means (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*). The Sūtra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a profound samādhi, remaining unmoving with right mindfulness. Observing with wisdom as it truly is, he arose calmly from that samādhi.
Having arisen, he immediately addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!

The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter. That which the Tathāgata has realized cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others."

Why is this? Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already personally attended upon, served, and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas; at the abodes of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddhas, he has fully practiced all the dharmas of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cultivated by those Buddhas.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, practiced with courageous diligence; his deeds are accomplished and his fame is universally renowned.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has ultimately accomplished a most rare and marvelous dharma. Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata is able to know the dharma that is difficult to understand.

Śāriputra, as for this dharma that is difficult to understand, it refers to the underlying intent of what the Buddha-Tathāgatas teach according to what is appropriate; this is something that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot know.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery in explaining causes.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has accomplished various skillful means, various forms of knowledge and vision, various modes of mindfulness and contemplation, and various modes of expression. Śāriputra!

Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings in various places, employing countless skillful means to guide sentient beings from their attachments so that they may attain liberation.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, and skillful means have reached the other shore. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, unobstructed and unhindered; he has fully perfected the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the faculties, the strengths, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the samāpattis.
Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have deeply entered the boundless and have accomplished all unprecedented dharmas. Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and expound all dharmas in various ways, using gentle and supple speech that delights the hearts of the multitude.
Enough, Śāriputra!
There is no need to say more,
Śāriputra! The Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand teaching.
Śāriputra! Only Buddhas speak the Dharma to Buddhas; the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are able to know the ultimate reality of that Dharma. Śāriputra!
Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, knows all dharmas.
Śāriputra! Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is able to expound all dharmas.
What are phenomena? In what way are they phenomena?
What are phenomena like?
What are the characteristics of phenomena? What is the essence of phenomena?

What are they, how are they, what do they resemble, what are their characteristics, and what is their essence? Regarding all such phenomena, the Tathāgata perceives them directly; he does not fail to perceive them.
The commentary states:

"At that time, the World-Honored One entered a profound samādhi, remaining unmoving in right mindfulness; with wisdom as it truly is, he observed from within samādhi and arose with composure. Having arisen, he immediately addressed Śāriputra. This demonstrates that the Tathāgata has attained the power of mastery, and that no one can startle or awaken the Tathāgata while he is in meditative concentration.
For what reason was the Venerable Śāriputra alone addressed, and not the other śrāvakas?
It is because his profound wisdom accords with that of the Tathāgata.
For what reason were the bodhisattvas not informed?
There are five reasons:
first, because it was a matter that concerned the śrāvakas.
Second, it is for the sake of causing those śrāvakas who have turned their minds to incline toward great enlightenment;
third, it is to protect the śrāvakas from fear and weakness;
fourth, it is to cause other people to reflect upon this with wholesome mindfulness.
Fifth, it is so that the śrāvakas will not give rise to the thought that they have already accomplished what was to be done.

As for the statement, "The wisdom of all Buddhas is extremely profound and immeasurable," it is intended to cause the great assembly to develop a mind of reverence and a desire to hear the Tathāgata’s teaching to the ultimate degree.
Regarding the term "profound," it should be understood that it reveals two kinds of profound meanings. What are these two?
First is the profundity of realization, which refers to the fact that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
Second is the profundity of the Āgamas, meaning that the gateways of wisdom are profound and immeasurable.
"Profound" is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); the others are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
The realization of profundity is manifested in five ways:
first, profundity of meaning, which refers to the basis of what kind of meaning is profound;
second, profundity of substantial entity; [and so forth].
Third, the profundity of internal realization;
fourth, the profundity of the basis;
fifth, the unsurpassed profundity.
What is profound? It is great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Great enlightenment is so called because it is the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* realized by the Tathāgata.
Why is it profound? It is called profound because it cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others.
As for the term "wisdom," it refers to the meaning of all modes and all-knowledge.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others."
Regarding the profoundness of the Āgamas, there are eight manifestations:

first, the profoundness of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting, as the sūtra states: "He has already drawn near to, made offerings to, and served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas."

Second is the profundity of practice, as the sūtra states: "In the presence of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas, one has fully practiced all the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cultivated by those buddhas."
Third is the profundity of the practice of the fruit, as the sūtra states:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has already accomplished what was to be done through courageous diligence over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas."
Fourth is the profound mind of increasing merit, as the sutra says, "His fame is heard everywhere.
Fifth is the profound mind of delightful and sublime matters, as the sutra says, "Śāriputra!"
"Because the Tathāgata has ultimately accomplished the most rare and marvelous dharmas.
Sixth is the unsurpassed profundity, as the sūtra says:
"Śāriputra, the dharma that is difficult to understand, the Tathāgata is able to know it."

Seventh is "entering the profound. To enter the profound means that the meaning of the names, phrases, and sentences is difficult to grasp; because it abides in its own sustaining power and differs from the causal teachings expounded by non-Buddhists, it is called "profound."
As the sūtra states: "Śāriputra!

Regarding the dharma that is difficult to understand, the intent behind the teachings of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, as they are expounded according to what is appropriate, is difficult to understand.

Eighth is the profundity of the maintenance and sustenance performed in a manner not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as the sūtra states: "That which cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like."
