This concludes the remainder of the "Chapter on Expedient Means. Thus, having already explained the perfection of the merits of the Sublime Dharma, one should now understand the explanation of the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of the merits of a Dharma-preacher.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For what reason? Śāriputra!
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery in explaining causes."
The Tathāgata accomplishes four kinds of merit, and is therefore able to deliver sentient beings. What are these four?
The first is the accomplishment of abiding, as the sutra says: "Śāriputra!..."
"Because the Tathāgata has accomplished various skillful means.
These various skillful means refer to everything from descending from Tuṣita Heaven down to manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa.
Second is the accomplishment of teaching and transformation, as stated in the sutra: "various knowledges and views.
These various knowledges and views demonstrate the various causes of defilement and purity.
Third is the ultimate accomplishment of merit, as stated in the sutra: "various recollections and contemplations.
These various recollections and contemplations refer to the causes and conditions for accomplishing those dharmas, because they correspond to the Dharma.
Fourth is the accomplishment of teaching, as stated in the sutra: "by means of various modes of expression.

"Various modes of expression" refers to employing the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) to teach by relying on whichever names, phrases, and syllables are appropriate, and according to whatever sentient beings are capable of receiving the teaching.

Furthermore, there is another meaning: "various skillful means" refers to the manifestation of the various faults of all the heterodox teachings of external paths through various skillful means, and the manifestation of the various merits of all the true teachings of the Buddhas through various skillful means.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra!

Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded verbal teachings and used innumerable skillful means to guide sentient beings from their various attachments so that they may attain liberation."
Furthermore, "innumerable skillful means" refers to employing skillful means to cause entry into all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to severing all doubts.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to causing entry into superior and transcendent wisdom.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to employing the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation.

Regarding "points of attachment," these are attachments to various locations: one may be attached to the various realms (*dhātu*), or attached to the various stages (*bhūmi*), or attached to the various factors (*aṅga*), or attached to the various vehicles (*yāna*).
"Attachment to the various realms" means attachment to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

"Attachment to the various stages" means attachment to the realms; it refers to relying on samādhi to grasp the stages of meditative concentration, from the stage of the first dhyāna up to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as grasping the stage of the attainment of cessation and so forth.
"Attachment to the various categories" refers to attachment to the categories of the laity and the renunciants.
Attachment to the category of the laity refers to attachment to one's own kind performing various activities, such as holding wrong views and so forth.
"Attachment to the category of renunciation" refers to attachment to fame, gain, various discursive thoughts, afflictions, and so forth.
"Attachment to the vehicles" refers to attachment to the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Those who adhere to the Śrāvaka vehicle delight in upholding the precepts of the Hīnayāna, seeking the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and so forth.

"Attachment to the Mahāyāna" refers to attachment to gain, offerings, honor, and so forth, as well as attachment to the conceptual observation of the various characteristics of phenomena up to the stage of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, regarding the various types of knowledge and vision: it is because one’s own body has accomplished an inconceivable, supreme, and wondrous state that is equal to those of all śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, and skillful means have reached the other shore.
To have reached the other shore means that he surpasses all other bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, regarding the various modes of mindfulness and contemplation, it is as the Sūtra states:

"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast, profound, and far-reaching; they are unobstructed and unimpeded. He is fully endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the faculties, the strengths, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the samāpattis. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, first, there is the accomplishment of those sentient beings who are ready to be transformed, because they achieve success by relying on spiritual friends;
second, there is the accomplishment of those sentient beings whose faculties are matured, so as to enable them to attain liberation;
third, there is the accomplishment of mastery over the powers, through the purification of subjugation.
Fourth, there are seven kinds of accomplishment:
first, various accomplishments, as the Sūtra states:
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have deeply entered the boundless and accomplished all unprecedented dharmas."

Second is the perfection of speech, which refers to attaining five kinds of exquisite vocal qualities for preaching the Dharma, as stated in the Sūtra: "The Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and expound all dharmas in various ways; his words are gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude."
Third is the accomplishment of characteristics, as the sutra states: "Stop, Śāriputra!
There is no need to speak further," because the minds of those sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma have already been satisfied.

Fourth is "capable of accomplishment," because all sentient beings who are capable of being transformed know that the Tathāgata has accomplished rare and supreme merits and is able to preach the Dharma.
As the Sūtra states: "Śāriputra!
The Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand.
Fifth is the accomplishment in immeasurable varieties, which cannot be fully described.
As the Sūtra states: "Śāriputra, it is only Buddhas speaking with Buddhas; the Tathāgatas are able to know the ultimate reality of that Dharma.
What is called "reality" (dharmatā) refers to the meaning of the unchanging essence of the Tathāgatagarbha-Dharmakāya.
Sixth is the accomplishment of the essence of awakening, because all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are realized and attained through the self-attestation of the Buddha-Tathāgata alone.
As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra!..."
"Only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows all dharmas.

Seventh, it is for the sake of accomplishing the teaching of the methods of practice according to the inclinations of sentient beings; this is because of such questions as "What are those dharmas? and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra!
Only the Buddha-Tathāgata can expound all dharmas," because he gathers in sentient beings through the first variety of dharma-gates.
The second is for the purpose of causing non-distraction;
the third is for the purpose of causing grasping;
the fourth is for the purpose of causing the attainment of liberation.
The fifth is to cause that practitioner to achieve the attainment of the remedial dharmas;
the sixth is to cause that practitioner to progress toward accomplishment;
the seventh is to cause the practitioner to attain non-retrogression in their practice.
These seven kinds of dharmas are for the sake of accomplishing the wholesome deeds performed by sentient beings themselves.
Furthermore, regarding those who are to be taught and transformed so that they may achieve accomplishment, two kinds of dharmas are provided to bring them to fulfillment.
What are these two? First, the bestowal of the Dharma of realization;
second, the bestowal of the Dharma of teaching.
First, bestowing the Dharma of realization so that it may be accomplished, which means bestowing it based on the Dharma of realization;
second, bestowing the Dharma of teaching so that it may be accomplished, which means teaching and bestowing it based on the Dharma of teaching.
These two types of dharmas are as previously explained.
Based on these two dharmas, what is the sequence for practicing them?
This should be understood as being restated from the preceding text.
Furthermore, based on the dharma to be realized, there are five kinds:
first, what kind of dharma;
second, how the dharma is.
Third, what kind of phenomena they are;
fourth, what characteristics these phenomena have;
and fifth, what essence these phenomena possess.
What are the dharmas? They are the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of the buddhas.
What is meant by "dharmas"? It refers to the arising of various matters for the purpose of exposition.
As for what constitutes the nature of the Dharma, it is because one attains purity by means of three doors.
As for what constitutes the characteristic of the Dharma, it refers to the fact that the three meanings constitute a single-characteristic Dharma.
As for what constitutes the essence of the Dharma, it is because there is no dual essence.
"Non-dual essence" means that the immeasurable vehicles are in fact only the single Buddha-vehicle, as there are no two vehicles.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
"what dharma" refers to dharmas such as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is meant by "dharmas"? It refers to dharmas of causal conditions, dharmas that are not of causal conditions, and so forth.
What is meant by "resembling dharmas"? It refers to dharmas that are permanent, dharmas that are impermanent, and so forth.
As for the nature of phenomena (*lakṣaṇadharma*), it refers to the three characteristics of arising and so forth, and the three characteristics of non-arising and so forth.
As for the substance of phenomena (*svabhāvadharma*), it refers to the substance of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and that which is not the substance of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, what is meant by "dharmas of such a nature"? It refers to impermanent dharmas, conditioned dharmas, and dharmas arising from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, what is meant by "dharmas of such characteristics"? It refers to dharmas possessing characteristics such as visibility.

Furthermore, as for the essence of phenomena, it refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the grasper and the grasped; this is because the five aggregates constitute the collective essence of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*), and furthermore, because the five aggregates constitute the essence of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Furthermore, there is another meaning based on the teaching of the Dharma:
as for "what dharma," it refers to the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables;
as for "how the dharma," it refers to that which is taught by the Tathāgata.
What is the nature of the Dharma? It is that which is able to transform those who are capable of being transformed.
What are the characteristics of the Dharma? They are apprehended by means of sound, because that Dharma is apprehended by relying upon sound.
Regarding "the essence of phenomena," this refers to the essence of conventional designations, because it is the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
From this point onward, there follows an exposition based on the manifestation of three types of meanings: first, the meaning of certainty;
[second, the meaning of non-attainment; third, the meaning of non-duality].
Second is doubt regarding the meaning;
third is that one should thoroughly understand the basis upon which doubt regarding the meaning arises.

As for the definitive meaning, there are śrāvakas who, through skillful means, attain realization of the profound Dharma and develop a mind of certainty, because they have attained the realization of the *upāya-nirvāṇa* within the path of the śrāvakas.
These two kinds of realized dharmas demonstrate both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
As the sutra states: "At that time, among the great assembly were various śrāvakas, arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who, in succession, even attained this dharma and reached nirvāṇa."
Regarding "doubtful meaning," this refers to that which the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are unable to know, and therefore give rise to doubt.
As it says in the sutra: "Yet they do not know where this meaning leads."

Regarding the doubt concerning the object: having heard the Tathāgata say that the liberation of the śrāvakas and one’s own liberation are neither different nor distinct, one consequently gives rise to doubt. This means that the one who generates the doubt experiences uncertainty regarding the cause of its arising, thinking:
"What is this matter?"
What does this mean?

It means that because the Tathāgata repeatedly teaches the profound realm—speaking of what is profound first and speaking of what is profound later—it differs from that of the śrāvakas; for this reason, doubt arises.
As the sutra states: "At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly, proceeded in sequence and spoke these verses.
From this point onward, the following is explained based on the manifestation of four matters;
the first is the resolute mind.
Second, the prediction based on causes;
third, the prediction by taking up [the vow];
fourth, the prediction by bestowing [it]. These should be well understood.
What is the resolute mind?
It is that which causes those who have already become terrified to sever their terror; because it benefits these two kinds of persons, the Tathāgata possesses a resolute mind.
This fear should be understood as fivefold:
first, the fear of loss. This refers to sentient beings of the Hīnayāna who take what they have heard literally, denigrating the Mahāyāna by giving rise to such a thought:
"The Tathāgata has declared that the fruit of arhatship is ultimate nirvāṇa."
"I shall ultimately attain such nirvāṇa," and for this reason, the Arhat does not enter nirvāṇa;
thus they experience fear and terror.

Second is the fear and terror of manifold activities, which refers to sentient beings of the Mahāyāna who, upon hearing that the Bodhisattva path involves vast numbers of kalpas and various ascetic practices, give rise to this thought:
The Buddha-way is long and distant; for immeasurable and boundless kalpas, I have practiced the bodhisattva path and endured much hardship and suffering.
Because of such reflections, a sense of alarm and fear arises, and for this reason, the thought of adopting a different vehicle (yāna) is produced.

Such is the fear. Third is the fear of perversion, which refers to the mind’s conceptualization of various views of selfhood (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—such as "I" and "mine"—and other unwholesome dharmas. Such is the fear.
Fourth is remorse and trepidation in the mind; that is to say, the Venerable Śāriputra and others gave rise to such thoughts, saying:
"I ought not to have practiced or realized such a Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle."
Having repented in this way, the mind ceases of its own accord; this very mental repentance is called "alarm and fear.
This meaning should be understood.
Fifth is the alarm and fear of deception, which refers to the thought arising in a śrāvaka of overweening pride:
"How can the Tathāgata deceive us?"—thus they were struck with such terror.
Regarding the bestowal of the prediction, it is as the sutra says: "Stop, stop, Śāriputra!"
"There is no need to speak further;
for if this matter were spoken, all the devas and humans in the world would give rise to alarm and fear.
There are three meanings to why those who receive this prediction of enlightenment all experience such alarm and fear:
First, it is because he wishes to cause that great assembly to investigate the profound and wondrous realm;
second, it is because he wishes to cause that great assembly to give rise to a mind of reverence and ultimately desire to hear what the Tathāgata speaks;
third, it is because he wishes to cause those śrāvakas of overweening pride to abandon their seats and depart.
The second invitation demonstrates how the Buddhas of the past, in immeasurable numbers, transformed sentient beings.
This is because the sutra states: "In this assembly, there were countless successions [of beings], up until those who, upon hearing what the Buddha taught, gave rise to reverent faith."
The third request demonstrates that the present Buddha is currently transforming sentient beings.
As the sutra states: "Those in this assembly who are like us, and so on in succession, shall for a long night be at peace and receive much benefit."
Regarding the bestowing of predictions: this refers to Śāriputra and others wishing to receive their predictions.
As the sutra says: "The Buddha told Śāriputra:
'You have already made three requests; how could I not speak?'"
"Listen attentively now," and so forth. Regarding the bestowing of prediction (vyākaraṇa), it should be understood that there are six types:
first, causing those who have not heard [the Dharma] to hear it;...
Second, the teaching;
third, the basis of which meaning;
fourth, causing [beings] to abide [therein].
Fifth is according to the Dharma;
sixth is prohibition.
To cause those who have not heard [the teaching] to hear it, as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra!..."
Because such a wondrous Dharma is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals, like the udumbara flower, and so forth.
As for "preaching," it is as stated in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra!..."
"By means of countless skillful methods, through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, I have expounded all dharmas"—it is because of such statements as these.
"Various causes and conditions" refers to the so-called Three Vehicles.
Those three vehicles exist only as names, phrases, and verbal expressions; they do not possess actual reality, because that actual reality is inexpressible.
Regarding the meaning upon which they depend, it is as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra!..."
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great matter.
Because of such statements as these, one should properly understand the "one great matter" by means of four kinds of meanings.
What are the four? First is the meaning of unsurpassedness: there is nothing else that can surpass the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
As the sūtra says: "Because he wishes to open the Buddha's knowledge and vision so that sentient beings may know and attain purity, he appears in the world."

Regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: because the Tathāgata is able to realize and know their profound meaning as it truly is, these two share the same meaning; that is to say, the Dharma-body of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is equal to that of the Buddha.
As the sutra states: "He appears in the world in order to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Regarding the equality of the Dharma-body: it is because there is no distinction between the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body.
Third is the lack of understanding of the meaning, which refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, because they are unable to know that true state.
This statement regarding not knowing the true state means that they do not know that the ultimate is solely the One Buddha Vehicle.
As it says in the Sūtra: "He appears in the world in order to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Fourth, he causes them to realize the stage of non-retrogression, manifesting his desire to bestow immeasurable wisdom and activity.
This is as stated in the sutra: "I appear in the world in order to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, "to demonstrate" means to cause those bodhisattvas who harbor doubts to understand how to practice according to reality.
Furthermore, "entering into awakening" means causing those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment to do so, and causing those who have already resolved to enter the Dharma.
Moreover, "awakening" means causing beings among the non-Buddhist sects to give rise to realization.
Furthermore, "those who enter" refers to those who have attained the fruits of the Śrāvaka’s Lesser Vehicle being led to enter into Bodhi.
"Those who abide" refers to what is stated in the Sūtra:
"Śāriputra, it is solely for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle that I preach the Dharma to sentient beings."
Regarding "according to the Dharma," it is as stated in the sutra: "Śāriputra!

The Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various parables, causes and conditions, and the skillful means of mindfulness and contemplation, have preached the Dharma; all these teachings are for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. It is because of such passages that this is so.
Regarding the use of analogies: it is like how, depending upon the cow, there come to be milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the finest cream (*sarpis*).
Among these five flavors, the finest cream is supreme; the Hīnayāna is not its equal, being like milk, whereas the Mahāyāna is the most excellent, being like the finest cream.
This analogy clarifies that the Mahāyāna is supreme because even the śrāvakas and others share in the sense of the Mahāyāna’s supremacy.

As for their commonality with the śrāvakas: herein it is demonstrated that the nature of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is identical to that of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, for the dharmakāya is equal and without distinction.
All these meanings are metaphorical demonstrations of the principles of causes and conditions, as previously explained.
As for "contemplation," it refers to the contemplations of the selflessness of persons and so forth within the truths of the Hīnayāna;

and within the truths of the Mahāyāna, it refers to the various contemplations of *tathatā* (suchness), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), as well as the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.

Regarding "expedient means" (upāya): in the Hīnayāna, it refers to contemplating the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana) to become weary of suffering, leave suffering, and attain liberation;
in the Mahāyāna, it refers to the various pāramitās and the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) used to gather oneself and others, serving as beneficial remedies.
As for "negation," it is as stated in the sūtra:
"Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions there are not even two vehicles, let alone three," and so forth.

Regarding "there are no two vehicles": this means there is no *nirvāṇa* attained by the two vehicles; rather, it is only when the Tathāgata realizes great *bodhi* and brings all wisdom to ultimate fulfillment that it is called Great *Nirvāṇa*. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others do not possess the dharma of *nirvāṇa*, for there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
The Single Buddha Vehicle is explained based on four kinds of meanings, which should be well understood.

The Tathāgata relies upon these six kinds of predictions; therefore, what was previously stated—namely, what kind of dharma, how the dharma, what the dharma resembles, what the characteristics of the dharma, and what the essence of the dharma are—is thus demonstrated.
What is the Dharma? It refers to that which has never been heard before.
How is the Dharma expressed? It refers to its manifestation through various words, phrases, and parables.
What is the nature of the Dharma? It is said to be solely for the sake of the one great matter.
As for the characteristics of the Dharma, it is because the various Buddha-dharmas are taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
As for the essence of the Dharma, it is because there is only the essence of the One Vehicle.
The essence of the One Vehicle is the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess this essence of the equal Dharma-body, because their causal practices and contemplations differ.
From this point onward, it should be understood that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is intended to sever four kinds of doubt.
What are these four doubts?
First, the doubt as to when [the teaching] was spoken;
2. The doubt: How is it known that this person is one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?
3. The doubt: How is he capable of preaching [this]?
4. The doubt: How is it that the Tathāgata does not utter falsehoods?
Regarding "at what time it was spoken": in order to sever this doubt, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, at a certain time, gave rise to various skillful means to preach the Dharma.
As the sutra says: "Śāriputra!"
"The Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities, namely the turbidity of the eon," and so forth.

How is it known that such a person is one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*)? The Tathāgata does not preach the various dharmas for those who possess overweening pride; how then is it known that they are persons of overweening pride?
To sever this doubt, it is as stated in the Sūtra: "If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship, yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible," and so forth.

Regarding "how one is fit to be spoken to": having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, one gives rise to a mind of slander, thinking, "The Tathāgata must be someone unfit to be spoken to; why then has he not become someone unfit to be spoken to?"
To sever this doubt, it is as the sutra says: "Except after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one," and so forth.

As for how the Tathāgata does not commit false speech: since the Tathāgata previously taught the Dharma in one way and now teaches the Dharma in another way, how is it that the Tathāgata does not become a speaker of falsehood?
To sever this doubt, as the sutra states: "Śāriputra!

You all should with single-minded resolve believe, understand, accept, and uphold the Buddha’s words; the words of the Tathāgatas are not false. There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle."

Regarding the statement, "Even those who, as children playing, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood," this means that the roots of goodness cultivated by those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and practice the bodhisattva path are capable of realizing enlightenment; it is not something that can be attained by ordinary worldlings or by those śrāvakas fixed in their destiny who have never originally resolved to attain bodhicitta.
In this manner, even down to such acts as slightly bowing the head, it is all likewise so.
Chapter Three: The Parable The Venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses:
“With a golden body and the thirty-two marks, Possessing the ten powers and various liberations,”
Within this same single Dharma, I have failed to attain these things:
the eighty kinds of minor marks, the eighteen unique qualities,
and such meritorious attributes as these— I have lost them all.
The commentary states:
What meaning does this verse reveal?
The Venerable Śāriputra reproaches himself, saying:

I do not see the Buddhas, nor do I go to the presence of the Buddhas to hear their teaching of the Dharma; I do not make offerings to or revere the Buddhas, and I lack any activity for the benefit of sentient beings; thus, I have regressed from the Dharma I had not yet attained.
The Venerable Śāriputra reproached himself in this manner.

His failure to see the Buddha was a manifestation of his not seeing the marks of a Great Man belonging to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, because he had failed to give rise to a mind of reverence and offerings.
Going to the place where the Buddha is, it is because he manifests the power to teach and transform sentient beings.
Emitting golden light, it is because he manifests that by seeing the Buddha’s own body and other bodies, one obtains immeasurable merits.
The teaching of the Dharma is manifested in order to bring about the benefit of all sentient beings.
As for the powers (*bala*), they are manifested because when sentient beings have doubts, he relies upon the ten powers to sever those doubts.
Making offerings demonstrates the power to transform sentient beings.
The eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) demonstrate the removal of all obstacles.
Regarding "reverence," it demonstrates the production of immeasurable merit, for one attains liberation by relying on the Tathāgata’s teaching.

Because both the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) mean that all dharmas are entirely equal, the Venerable Śāriputra reproached himself, saying:
"I have not yet attained such a dharma."

Because there is regression regarding what has not yet been attained, from this point onward, seven similes are next presented for the sake of sentient beings who possess the nature of being defiled by the seven types of afflictions, in order to counteract the seven types of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); this meaning should be understood.

Furthermore, for those who are free from afflictions yet possess the three types of pride regarding defilement—namely, pride concerning meditative concentration (*samādhi*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the body (*kāya*)—the three kinds of equality are taught as their antidote.
This meaning should be understood.
Regarding the character "view" (見) found in the Dan edition below the word "body" (身): who are the seven types of sentient beings whose nature is defiled by fully developed afflictions?
First, those who seek power and influence;... [and so forth].
Second, those who seek the liberation of the śrāvaka;
third, those of the Mahāyāna;
fourth, those possessed of meditative concentration.
Fifth, those who are not fixed;
sixth, those who accumulate merit;
seventh, those who do not accumulate merit.
What are the seven kinds of conceited mind (*adhimāna*)?
What are the seven kinds of analogies used as their antidotes?

First is the conceited mind that seeks merit through inversion: this refers to seeking the tainted retributions of superior celestial or human realms while the various afflictions (*kleśa*) within the world are burning with intense intensity.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the parable of the burning house is taught.
Second, there are śrāvakas who possess a one-sided, fixed conceit of superiority, claiming that their own vehicle is no different from the Tathāgata’s vehicle; they thus grasp it erroneously.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the parable of the impoverished son is taught.
Third, there is the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) that is one-sidedly fixed upon the Mahāyāna, which gives rise to the thought:
"There is no separate vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Such is this inverted grasping.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the metaphor of the clouds and rain is taught.

Fourth, there are those with the conceit of overestimation (*abhimāna*) who claim what is unreal to be real; because they possess worldly *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, they conceive of what is not truly *nirvāṇa* as being *nirvāṇa*.
To counteract such erroneous grasping, it should be understood that the parable of the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇapurī*) is taught.

Fifth is the pride of distraction: although one actually lacks meditative concentration, one fails to realize that despite having roots of goodness in the Mahāyāna in the past, one does not seek the Mahāyāna because of this lack of realization. Within a narrow and inferior mind, one gives rise to false understanding, claiming it to be the Supreme Vehicle; thus one grasps it erroneously.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the analogy of the tied jewel is taught.
Sixth is the conceit of possessing superior merit when one actually lacks it; hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma, they grasp it as non-Mahāyāna, thus taking it up erroneously.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the analogy of the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) giving away the bright jewel from within his topknot is taught.

Seventh is the conceit of superiority (*abhimāna*) regarding non-existent virtues: one has never cultivated the roots of goodness for the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), yet upon hearing of the Supreme Vehicle, one does not accept it as supreme in one's mind, thus grasping it erroneously.
To counteract this, it should be understood that the analogy of the physician is taught.

The foremost person is one who, by means of various roots of goodness, samādhis, merits, and skillful means, first causes others to rejoice within the world, and subsequently leads them into Great Nirvāṇa.
The second person unifies the three vehicles into one, thereby causing entry into the Mahāyāna.

The third person causes them to know that the various vehicles are taught by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas with equal intent, so that sprouts may grow according to the seeds of the roots of goodness of sentient beings.
As for the fourth person, it is because he employs skillful means to cause them to enter the city of nirvāṇa.
The city of nirvāṇa refers to the city of the various dhyānas and samādhis;
having passed through that city, he then causes them to enter the city of great parinirvāṇa.
As for the fifth person, it is because one causes them to recollect all their past roots of goodness and subsequently instructs them to enter samādhi.

As for the sixth person, it is because one teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma, and since this dharma-gate is identical to the fulfillment of the practices of the ten stages, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas secretly bestow upon them a prophecy of enlightenment.
As for the seventh person, because their faculties are not yet fully matured, [the Buddha] manifests the measure of attaining nirvana in this way so that they may reach maturity.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has taught seven types of analogies.
What are the three kinds of people free from afflictions and the three kinds of defiled conceit?
They are so called because of their three kinds of perverted faith. What are these three?
First, believing in the diversity of the various vehicles;
second, believing in the distinction between the mundane world and nirvana;
third, believing in the distinctness of one's own body and the bodies of others.
To counteract these three types of defiled pride, one should know that three kinds of equality are taught.
What are the names of these three kinds of equality?
How do they serve as antidotes?

First is the equality of the vehicle (*yāna-samatā*), which means bestowing the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon the śrāvakas; for there is only the single Great Vehicle and no second vehicle, as this vehicle is equal and without distinction.
Second is the equality of the mundane world and nirvana; because when the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna entered nirvana, the mundane world and nirvana were equal to one another, without distinction.

Third is the equality of the body: although the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has already entered parinirvāṇa, he again manifests his physical form, because one's own body and the bodies of others are equal as the Dharma-body, without distinction.

Thus, these three types of persons who are free from afflictions yet possess a mind stained by pride perceive the differences between their own bodies and those of others; because they do not know that the Buddha-nature and Dharma-body of both self and others are entirely equal, they claim, "I have realized this Dharma, whereas that person has not attained this remedy. It should be understood that these are the ones for whom the Buddhas bestow predictions of enlightenment, as is the case with the śrāvakas.
Question: Are those śrāvakas and others given the prediction of enlightenment because they will truly become Buddhas,
or are they given the prediction despite not becoming Buddhas?
If he has truly attained Buddhahood, for what reason would the Bodhisattva have cultivated and accumulated immeasurable varieties of merit over immeasurable kalpas?
If he has not attained Buddhahood, how could one grant him a false prediction of enlightenment?

Answer: When those śrāvakas and others receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), they attain a mind of certainty; this does not mean that the śrāvakas have realized the *dharmatā-tathāgata*.

Based on those three kinds of equality, the One Vehicle Dharma is taught; because the Buddha-dharmakāya and the śrāvaka-dharmakāya are equal and without distinction, the prediction is granted, yet it does not mean they are already fully endowed with the merit of cultivation.
Therefore, the Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with merit, whereas the Śrāvakas are not yet so endowed.
Regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), six instances are manifested: five are predictions for Buddhas, and one is a prediction for a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s bestowal of predictions: for those such as Śāriputra and Mahākāśyapa, who were well known to the assembly and had distinct names, he bestowed predictions individually.
For the five hundred such as Pūrṇa and the twelve hundred, since they shared the same name, he bestowed the predictions all at once.
Those who are in training and those beyond training all share the same title, and furthermore, they are not widely known to the public; therefore, they are given the prediction together.
As for the Tathāgata’s granting of a separate prediction to Devadatta, it is to demonstrate that the Tathāgata harbors no enmity or ill will.

As for the bestowing of predictions upon the bhikṣuṇīs and the various goddesses, it is to demonstrate that women—whether remaining at home or having left the household life—can all realize the fruit of Buddhahood by practicing the bodhisattva path; therefore, they are granted these predictions.
Regarding the prediction for bodhisattvas, it should be understood as manifested in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" below.
As for the statement, "I do not slight you; you shall all become buddhas," this is manifested because all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
Regarding those śrāvakas who receive the prediction of enlightenment, there are four types of śrāvakas:
first, the śrāvaka of fixed destiny; second, the śrāvaka of overweening pride; [third, the śrāvaka of uncertain destiny; fourth, the śrāvaka who turns toward the Mahāyāna].
Third, the śrāvakas who have regressed from the bodhicitta;
fourth, the śrāvakas who are emanations.
Regarding these two types of śrāvakas, the Tathāgata bestows predictions: namely, those who are emanations and those who, having regressed, subsequently resolve their minds anew upon bodhicitta.

Regarding the two types of śrāvakas—the those who are fixed in their destiny and the those with overweening pride—they are not granted a prediction [of enlightenment] because their faculties have not yet matured.
As for the bodhisattvas who are granted a prediction, it is because [the Buddha] employs skillful means to cause them to resolve upon bodhicitta.
Furthermore, based on what meaning does the Buddha teach that the three vehicles are called the one vehicle?
It is based on the meaning of sameness; for this reason, he bestows the prediction of great enlightenment upon all śrāvakas.
As for the meaning of sameness, it is because the Dharma-body of the Buddhas and the Dharma-body of the śrāvakas are mutually equal and without distinction.

Because the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others differ, there are distinctions between them; since those two vehicles are not the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata has declared that they are not separate from my own body in terms of the unsurpassed meaning. This meaning is not taught within the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because they are unable to understand it as it truly is.
For this reason, the bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path do not act in vain.
Regarding the "unsurpassed meaning," other sūtras clarify this unsurpassed meaning; briefly, there are ten kinds of this unsurpassed meaning, which should be understood.
What are the ten? First, because it demonstrates the supremacy of the seed, the simile of rain is taught.

Regarding the statement, "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path," this means that for those who have regressed from the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) and then resolved upon it again, the roots of goodness previously cultivated are not destroyed, as they are identical to those obtained later.
Second, because it manifests the supremacy of practice, it speaks of the past lives of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and so forth.
Third, because it manifests the supremacy of the increase of power, it speaks of the parable of the merchant leader.
Fourth, in order to manifest and cause understanding of the unsurpassed, he speaks the parable of the tied jewel.
Fifth, in order to manifest the supremacy of the pure land, he manifests the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
Sixth, because he manifests the teaching of the unsurpassed, he speaks the parable of the bright jewel within the topknot.
Seventh, because he manifests the unsurpassed transformation of sentient beings, immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others emerge from the earth.

Eighth, because it manifests the attainment of supreme great enlightenment, it manifests the three kinds of Buddha-enlightenment: First, it manifests the enlightenment of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body Buddha), manifesting according to what should be seen by others. As the sutra says: "All say that the Tathāgata departed from the palace of the Śākya clan and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Second, it manifests the enlightenment of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward-body Buddha), which is the realization of eternal nirvāṇa upon fulfilling the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). As the sutra says: "Good son!... [The passage continues: "Because he has fulfilled the practices of the ten stages, he has attained the realization of eternal nirvāṇa. Thus, the *saṃbhogakāya* is the manifestation of the reward-body Buddha's enlightenment. Third, it manifests the enlightenment of the *dharmakāya* (truth-body Buddha), which is the realization of the ultimate reality of all phenomena. As the sutra says: "Good son! Because he has fully realized the ultimate reality of all phenomena, he has attained the realization of eternal nirvāṇa. Thus, the *dharmakāya* is the manifestation of the truth-body Buddha's enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata manifests the three kinds of Buddha-enlightenment. Furthermore, because he manifests these three kinds of Buddha-enlightenment, he manifests the attainment of supreme great enlightenment. This is called the "manifestation of the attainment of supreme great enlightenment. This is the eighth point. Regarding the characteristics of the three realms: it means that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of nirvāṇa, because the tathāgatagarbha is not separate from the realm of sentient beings.
"There is no birth-and-death, whether in decline or emergence" means that its nature is eternally constant, cool, and unchanging.

The phrase "neither abiding in the world nor entering parinirvāṇa" means that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is True Suchness (tathatā), is neither identical with the realm of sentient beings nor separate from the realm of sentient beings.
"Neither real nor unreal, neither such nor different" means that it is free from four kinds of characteristics, for that which possesses four kinds of characteristics is impermanent.
"Not seeing the triple world as the triple world is seen [by others]" means that while the Buddha-Tathāgata is able to see and realize the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā*, ordinary beings do not see it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata perceives clearly and without error.

As for the statement, "I originally practiced the bodhisattva path and even now it is not yet fulfilled," this is because of his original vow; since the realm of sentient beings is not yet exhausted, that vow is not yet finalized.
That the statement was not yet complete does not mean that *bodhi* is incomplete.

Regarding the phrase "the lifespan attained is twice the aforementioned number," this passage demonstrates the permanence of the Tathāgata’s life; because it employs skillful means to manifest a great number, it exceeds the aforementioned quantity and cannot be calculated.

Regarding the manifestation of the stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna as the purity of all buddha-fields: it is because within the realm of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all Buddhas, various jewels are manifested in an intermingled and ornamental array.
There are eight manifestations:
first, the stupa;
second, the measurement.
Third is brevity;
fourth is maintaining and upholding;
fifth is manifesting immeasurable Buddhas.
Sixth, freedom from defilement;
seventh, many jewels;
eighth, sitting together in a single stūpa.
A "stūpa" (tā) signifies the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s śarīra remaining in the world.

Its "measure" (pramāṇa) is the skillful manifestation of the pure adornments of all buddha-fields; it is produced by supramundane, pure, and untainted roots of goodness, and is not produced by mundane, tainted roots of goodness.
"Briefly" means that it manifests the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna as a single entity that encompasses the true Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
"Abiding and maintaining" means that it manifests the sovereign power of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Manifesting immeasurable Buddhas means manifesting that the various karmas performed by this and that [Buddha] are without distinction.
Being far removed from defilement means manifesting that all Buddha-lands are equally pure.
"Prabhūtaratna" (Much-Treasure) signifies that all buddha-lands manifest as identical in their true nature (*dharmatā*).

"Sitting together in the same stupa" signifies that whether they be transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), dharma-buddhas, or reward-buddhas (*vipāka-buddha*), they all act in concert to accomplish the great task.
